title: Apple, Uber and Elections Headline Week
summary: Can Apple, Uber and Palantir turn this stock market around? It sure needs it. Worries about excessive AI spending tanked Google’s stock last week and sent the Nasdaq Composite to its worst month since March 2025. While the major indexes are still in the green for the year, a few more days like Friday’s could change that. Fortunately, we have a handful of earnings that might temper the gloom. Palantir Technologies, which reports Monday, has told investors to expect an 83% jump in the third quarter from the year-ago period. That’s a slowdown from the second quarter’s blistering 93% growth . But at least investors will get a reprieve from enormous capital expenditures. Palantir only spent $22 million in capex in the first half. As for Apple, it’s already warned investors that supply constraints for advanced chip manufacturing would contribute to slower revenue growth, to a range of  9% to 11% in the September quarter from a year ago, slower than its 16% growth in the June quarter. Apple has also forecast iPhone revenue growth in the mid-teens versus 22% in the June quarter. An improvement on that outlook could buoy the mood. On the other hand, a sharper slowdown in growth from either companies could give investors another reason to sell tech stocks.

title: Candidates Backing Data Center Pauses Could Win in Up to 15 Governor’s Races
summary: As data centers have gone from obscurity to the top of voters’ minds, midterm candidates are taking a stance on the issue. The fight is most heated in races for governor, the office that has shown the most power to limit data centers on a broad scale. Whichever candidates win, more doors are likely to close on the industry, leaving it with fewer places to build and higher costs where it still can. In 21 of the 36 states electing a governor on Tuesday, at least one major-party nominee backs a data center moratorium, according to The Information’s analysis of candidate platforms and public statements. Both nominees back pauses in five states (Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, Oregon and Texas), and a candidate promising a pause is likely to win in three (Maine, New Mexico and New York), based on recent polls. In seven more, it could be a close race between a candidate who backs a pause and one who doesn’t (Alaska, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Wisconsin and Vermont). Those 15 states are home to more than a third of the U.S. population.
